name: BoolQ
description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer that is either 'yes' or 'no'.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1, 2019.
rai:dataCollection: Data were gathered using the pipeline from Natural Questions with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results, after which the question and Wikipedia page were given to a human annotator. Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: deciding if the question was good (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; finding a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, or marking it not answerable; and finally marking whether the answer was yes or no. The dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Search, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages returned among the first five search results; additionally 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Unlike in Natural Questions, the dataset only uses questions marked as having a yes/no answer and pairs each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document. The authors combined 13k newly gathered questions with 3k questions from the Natural Questions training set, then split them into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set, ensuring questions from Natural Questions were always in the train set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified using a manually constructed set of indicator words and a sufficient-length requirement. Questions were only retained if a Wikipedia page appeared in the first five search results. Annotators filtered for good questions and answerable passages. The final dataset kept only questions marked as having a yes/no answer and used the selected passage rather than the full document to reduce ambiguity and keep inputs small enough for existing entailment models.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotators labeled question/article pairs in three steps. First, they judged whether the question was good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information, before seeing the Wikipedia page. Second, for good questions, they found a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question, or marked the question as not answerable if the article did not contain the requested information. Third, they marked whether the answer was yes or no.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess annotation quality, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples. When there was disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement, producing gold-standard labels. On these 110 examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Based on this agreement, the authors used singly annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Human annotators; three of the authors also labeled 110 randomly chosen examples for quality assessment.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Heuristic identification of likely yes/no questions using a manually constructed set of indicator words.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that the data and code are presented at https://goo.gl/boolq. No updating timeframe, maintainers, or deprecation policy are specified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to test models on answering naturally occurring yes/no questions that people genuinely want to answer, tying the benchmark to a practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common, comprising 62.31% in the train set. The paper also notes some correlation between question topic or type and the likelihood of a yes answer, and that some language patterns in passages may correlate with the answer.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has a class imbalance toward yes answers. Annotation quality analysis found ambiguous or debatable cases and some annotator misunderstandings. The paper notes that the analysis of inference categories may be slightly out of date because the dataset was updated after that analysis. The dataset uses selected passages rather than full documents, which reduces ambiguity but does not provide document-level context.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used as a reading comprehension benchmark for yes/no question answering and for training, development, and testing models. The paper defines train, dev, and test splits of 9.4k, 3.2k, and 3.2k examples respectively.
